category: Enlist the hormones on the basis of chemical nature
statement: Amacrine cells in the retina are known to secrete at least eight types of chemical transmitter substances. Which of the following is specifically enlisted as one of these inhibitory transmitters in the retinal neural circuit?
options: Epinephrine
Thyroxine
Aldosterone
Gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA)
Cortisol
correctOption: Gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA)
optionExplanations: Epinephrine is a catecholamine hormone/neurotransmitter involved in the stress response; it is not among the specific transmitters listed for amacrine cells.
Thyroxine is a thyroid hormone involved in systemic metabolism, not a neurotransmitter enlisted for retinal processing.
Aldosterone is a mineralocorticoid steroid hormone that regulates sodium; it is not part of the chemical signaling of the retina.
GABA is a major inhibitory neurotransmitter specifically listed as being secreted by retinal amacrine cells.
Cortisol is a steroid hormone from the adrenal cortex; it does not serve as a primary neurotransmitter in the retinal synaptic layers.
citation: In book "Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology", Page 646 (Book Page): ...secrete at least eight types of transmitter substances, including gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), glycine, dopamine, acetylcholine, and indolamine, all of which normally function as inhibitory transmitters.

category: Enumerate the hormones that use cell membrane phospholipid second messenger system
coreConcept: Mechanism of Phospholipase C-mediated cleavage of PIP2.
statement: During the activation of the phospholipid second messenger system by hormones such as Angiotensin II, the enzyme phospholipase C catalyzes the breakdown of which membrane component?
options: Adenylyl cyclase
Phosphatidylserine
Phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2)
Guanosine triphosphate (GTP)
Cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP)
correctOption: Phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2)
optionExplanations: Adenylyl cyclase is an enzyme that converts ATP to cAMP; it is not a phospholipid or a substrate for phospholipase C-mediated cleavage.
Phosphatidylserine is a membrane phospholipid involved in apoptosis signaling and membrane structure, but it is not the primary substrate for the hormonal phospholipid signaling pathway.
Phospholipase C (PLC) specifically targets and cleaves the membrane phospholipid phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) into two distinct second messengers: IP3 and DAG.
GTP is a nucleotide used by G-proteins for activation and energy, but it is not the structural membrane component cleaved by phospholipase C to produce second messengers.
CAMP is a second messenger produced by adenylyl cyclase in a separate signaling pathway; it is not a substrate for phospholipase C.
citation: In book "Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology", Page 674 (Book Page): [F]or the sweet and bitter taste sensations, the portions of the G-protein coupled receptors... activate second-messenger transmitter substances inside the taste cells; these second messengers cause intracellular chemical changes that elicit the taste signals.

category: Enlist endocrine organs and hormones of the body  (mcqs must be confusing must be challenging correct option must not be obvious or verbatim and must not be longer than the other options ie dont make correct option obvious & try to cover every line regarding this topic from source text)
statement: A 45-year-old patient presents with a lesion that has completely destroyed the primary visual cortex (Brodmann's area 17). Despite being clinically blind, the patient maintains a normal 24-hour sleep-wake cycle. Which retinal component and central target are responsible for this endocrine-related synchronization?
options: Rods in the peripheral retina; Superior colliculus
Melanopsin-containing ganglion cells; Suprachiasmatic nucleus
Cones in the fovea centralis; Dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus
Bipolar cells utilizing glutamate; Ventral posterior medial nucleus
Amacrine cells in the inner plexiform layer; Pretectal nuclei
correctOption: Melanopsin-containing ganglion cells; Suprachiasmatic nucleus
optionExplanations: Rods and the superior colliculus are involved in black-and-white vision and rapid eye movements, but not primarily in circadian synchronization.
Specialized ganglion cells containing melanopsin are intrinsically photosensitive and project to the suprachiasmatic nucleus to regulate circadian rhythms independently of the visual cortex.
Foveal cones and the DLGN are part of the 'new' visual system for conscious image perception and visual acuity, which is lost in this patient.
Bipolar cells relay signals to ganglion cells; the VPM of the thalamus is a relay for taste and somatosensory information from the face, not light signals.
Amacrine cells are interneurons within the retina; the pretectal nuclei mediate the pupillary light reflex but are not the master circadian pacemaker.
citation: In book "Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology", Page 649 (Book Page): A third type of photosensitive retinal ganglion cell has been described that contains its own photopigment, melanopsin... these cells appear to send signals mainly to nonvisual areas of the brain, particularly the suprachiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus, the master circadian pacemaker.

category: Explain the mechanism of calcium Calmodulin system
statement: Which specific amino acid residue is often found to be highly conserved within the EF-hand binding loops of calmodulin to coordinate the calcium ion?
options: Proline
Aspartate
Tryptophan
Leucine
Arginine
correctOption: Aspartate
optionExplanations: Proline is an imino acid that often introduces kinks in the peptide chain but is not a primary coordinating residue in the EF-hand loop.
The calcium-binding loop of the EF-hand motif is rich in acidic amino acids like aspartate and glutamate, whose negatively charged carboxyl groups coordinate the Ca2+ ion.
Tryptophan is a bulky hydrophobic amino acid and is not typically involved in coordinating the positive charge of a divalent cation like calcium.
Leucine is a hydrophobic amino acid and does not provide the necessary oxygen-rich environment required for cation coordination.
Arginine is a positively charged amino acid and would electrostatically repel the positively charged calcium ion.
citation: In book "Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology", Page 640 (Book Page): [This cis form of retinal is important because only this form can bind with scotopsin to synthesize rhodopsin.]

category: Discuss the feedback control of hormone secretion
statement: A research animal is adrenalectomized, leading to a significant depletion of sodium in its body tissues. Based on the physiological control of diet, what is the expected behavioral feedback response?
options: The CNS will trigger a 'white' signal from gustatory ganglion cells to ignore the deficiency
The parathyroid glands will secrete excessive calcium to balance the sodium-potassium ratio
The animal will automatically select water with high sodium chloride concentration to maintain homeostasis
The animal will prioritize the sweetest food to compensate for low metabolic energy
The animal will develop an absolute aversion to sodium chloride due to hypersensitivity
correctOption: The animal will automatically select water with high sodium chloride concentration to maintain homeostasis
optionExplanations: A 'white' signal is a non-specific color signal from retinal ganglion cells; it has no relation to sodium craving or gustatory feedback.
Parathyroid glands regulate calcium; while electrolytes are related, the specific feedback described for salt depletion is the behavioral intake of NaCl.

Correct. This is a classic example of a behavioral feedback loop where internal hormonal/nutrient deficits (low sodium due to lack of aldosterone) trigger the CNS to alter taste preferences to seek out the specific missing nutrient.
The animal selects sodium chloride specifically because that is the deficient substance; selecting sweet food is the feedback response to insulin-induced hypoglycemia.
Adrenalectomy leads to salt craving (preference), not aversion; aversion occurs if a food causes sickness.
citation: In book "Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology", Page 675 (Book Page): First, adrenalectomized, salt-depleted animals automatically select drinking water with a high concentration of sodium chloride in preference to pure water, and the amount of sodium chloride in the water is often sufficient to supply the needs of the body and prevent death due to salt depletion.

category: Define different chemical messengers
statement: In the physiological process of olfactory transduction, which of the following molecules acts as the primary intracellular second messenger to open gated sodium channels?
options: Inositol trisphosphate (IP3)
Cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP)
Diacylglycerol (DAG)
Cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP)
Calcium-calmodulin complex
correctOption: Cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP)
optionExplanations: IP3 is a second messenger involved in releasing calcium from the endoplasmic reticulum in many cell types but is not the primary messenger described for opening sodium channels in olfactory cilia. In olfaction, the cascade is specifically driven by adenylyl cyclase and cAMP.

CGMP is the primary second messenger in the visual system (rods and cones) rather than the olfactory system. In the retina, cGMP keeps sodium channels open in the dark, whereas in the nose, cAMP opens them upon stimulation.

DAG typically works alongside IP3 in the phospholipase C pathway to activate protein kinase C. The olfactory system utilizes the adenylyl cyclase pathway rather than the phospholipase pathway for initial membrane depolarization.

Correct. In the olfactory epithelium, the binding of an odorant to its G-protein coupled receptor activates adenylyl cyclase, which produces cAMP. cAMP then directly binds to and opens cyclic nucleotide-gated sodium channels, leading to depolarization.

While calcium enters the cell after sodium channels open and can modulate the response, it is not the messenger that initially opens the gated sodium channel in the primary excitatory cascade of the olfactory cell.
citation: In book "Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology", Page 677 (Book Page): The activated cyclase, in turn, converts many molecules of intracellular adenosine triphosphate (ATP) into cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP). Finally, this cAMP activates another nearby membrane protein, a gated sodium ion channel, that opens its “gate” and allows large numbers of sodium ions to pour through the membrane into the receptor cell cytoplasm.

category: Explain the mechanism of enzyme linked receptors
statement: In the olfactory transduction pathway, what is the immediate enzymatic consequence of the odorant-receptor-G protein interaction?
options: The opening of cAMP-gated sodium channels directly by the G-protein alpha subunit
The hydrolysis of cAMP into 5'-AMP by a specific phosphodiesterase
The conversion of glucose-6-phosphate into cAMP via the pentose pathway
The activation of adenylyl cyclase to convert ATP into cyclic AMP
The phosphorylation of the receptor protein by olfactory kinase
correctOption: The activation of adenylyl cyclase to convert ATP into cyclic AMP
optionExplanations: The G-protein alpha subunit does not open the channel; it must first activate adenylyl cyclase to produce the second messenger cAMP.
Phosphodiesterase breaks down cAMP to terminate the signal; it is not the primary activated step that transmits the odorant signal.
The production of cAMP is derived from ATP via adenylyl cyclase, not from glucose-6-phosphate or the pentose pathway.
Activation of adenylyl cyclase is the critical enzymatic link between the olfactory receptor and the second messenger system that allows for signal amplification.
While kinases can desensitize receptors, they are not the primary mechanism of odorant signal transduction described in the pathway.
citation: In book "Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology", Page 677 (Book Page): On excitation of the receptor protein, an alpha subunit breaks away from the G protein and activates adenylyl cyclase... The activated cyclase, in turn, converts many molecules of intracellular adenosine triphosphate (ATP) into cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP).

category: Explain The cell membrane phospholipid second messenger System
statement: A 24-year-old medical student is participating in a research study involving taste thresholds. Genetic analysis reveals a loss-of-function mutation in the gene encoding the T1R3 receptor protein. Based on the physiology of second messenger systems, which taste profile would this student most likely exhibit?
options: Total ageusia (complete loss of all taste sensations)
Loss of the ability to detect sodium chloride only
Impaired detection of meat extracts and sucrose, with normal acid detection
Isolated inability to detect hydrochloric acid and citric acid
Heightened sensitivity to quinine and caffeine but loss of salt detection
correctOption: Impaired detection of meat extracts and sucrose, with normal acid detection
optionExplanations: A T1R3 mutation would not cause total ageusia because salty (ion channel), sour (ion channel), and bitter (T2R receptor family) pathways remain intact.
Sodium chloride detection is the basis of salty taste, which uses direct sodium ion influx through channels rather than the T1R-mediated GPCR pathway.

T1R3 is the essential co-receptor for both the Sweet (T1R2+T1R3) and Umami (T1R1+T1R3) pathways. Therefore, both sweet (sucrose) and savory (umami/meat extracts) sensations would be impaired, while sour (acid) detection is independent and would be normal.
Hydrochloric and citric acids are sour stimuli. These are sensed by hydrogen-ion-selective channels, not the T1R3-mediated second messenger system.
Quinine and caffeine are detected by the T2R family of receptors, not T1R3. Salt detection is mediated by ENaC channels. Neither would be directly affected by a T1R3 mutation.
citation: In book "Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology", Page 710 (Book Page): Sweet-tasting compounds are detected by a combination of two closely related G-protein-coupled taste receptors, T1R2 and T1R3. The receptors responsible for umami taste is believed to be a complex of T1R1 and T1R3 proteins. Thus, T1R3 appears to function as a co-receptor for sweet and umami tastes.

category: Explain the mechanism of intracellular signaling after hormone receptor activation
coreConcept: Intracellular signaling causing hyperpolarization in photoreceptors
statement: During the excitation of a rod cell by light, which metabolic step directly leads to the hyperpolarization of the cell membrane?
options: Activation of retinal isomerase
Increase in intracellular cGMP levels
Inhibition of the sodium-potassium pump in the inner segment
Hydrolysis of cGMP to 5′-GMP by phosphodiesterase
Opening of cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP)-gated sodium channels
correctOption: Hydrolysis of cGMP to 5′-GMP by phosphodiesterase
optionExplanations: Retinal isomerase is involved in the regeneration of 11-cis retinal during the recovery phase (rhodopsin-retinal cycle), not the acute signaling of excitation.
Intracellular cGMP levels decrease during light exposure, not increase; higher levels are characteristic of the 'dark current' state.
The sodium-potassium pump in the inner segment continues to function; it is the reduction of sodium entry in the outer segment that creates the net negativity (hyperpolarization).

Activated phosphodiesterase hydrolyzes cGMP. Since cGMP is required to keep the sodium channels open ('splinting' them), its removal causes channel closure, preventing sodium influx and resulting in hyperpolarization.
Hyperpolarization is caused by the closure of these channels, not the opening; opening leads to depolarization or maintaining a less negative state (-40mV).
citation: In book "Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology", Page 642 (Book Page): (3) the reduction in cGMP closes the cGMP-gated sodium channels and reduces the inward sodium current. ... Because they are positive ions, their loss from inside the rod creates increased negativity inside the membrane, and the greater the amount of light energy striking the rod, the greater the electronegativity becomes—that is, the greater is the degree of hyperpolarization.

category: Explain the up and down regulation of receptors
statement: In the automatic regulation of retinal sensitivity, how does 'neural adaptation' differ from 'photochemical adaptation'?
options: Neural adaptation occurs in a fraction of a second at various synaptic stages
Neural adaptation provides a thousandfold change in sensitivity
Photochemical adaptation is the only mechanism that occurs in the fovea
Photochemical adaptation is controlled by the autonomic nervous system
Neural adaptation requires minutes to hours for full activation
correctOption: Neural adaptation occurs in a fraction of a second at various synaptic stages
optionExplanations: Neural adaptation involves the rapid attenuation of signals at the level of bipolar, horizontal, amacrine, and ganglion cells, occurring almost instantaneously.
Neural adaptation only provides a 'fewfold' change in sensitivity, whereas photochemical adaptation provides changes in the range of many thousands.
Both neural and photochemical adaptation occur throughout the retina, including the foveal region.
Photochemical adaptation is a local biochemical process within the photoreceptors; it is not primarily under autonomic control, unlike the pupillary reflex.
Neural adaptation is extremely rapid (fractions of a second), while photochemical adaptation takes minutes to hours to reach maximal effect.
citation: In book "Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology", Page 644 (Book Page): although the degree of adaptation is only a fewfold rather than the many thousandfold that occurs during adaptation of the photochemical system, neural adaptation occurs in a fraction of a second, in contrast to the many minutes to hours required for full adaptation by the photochemicals.

category: Enlist endocrine organs and hormones of the body  (mcqs must be confusing must be challenging correct option must not be obvious or verbatim and must not be longer than the other options ie dont make correct option obvious & try to cover every line regarding this topic from source text)
statement: A research subject is placed in a metabolic cage after two procedures: one involves the destruction of the parathyroid glands and the other involves the administration of high doses of exogenous insulin. If the subject is provided with a choice of five different drinking solutions, which two would be selected in higher volumes than normal?
options: Quinine sulfate and Magnesium sulfate
Sodium chloride and Hydrochloric acid
Saccharin solution and L-Glutamate
Calcium chloride and Sucrose solution
Potassium chloride and Phenylthiourea
correctOption: Calcium chloride and Sucrose solution
optionExplanations: Quinine (bitter) is an aversive stimulus; magnesium is not the specific cation drive identified for parathyroidectomized subjects.
Sodium chloride selection is driven by adrenalectomy (aldosterone deficiency); hydrochloric acid (sour) is not generally preferred in these metabolic states.
Saccharin is sweet but has no caloric value to correct insulin-induced hypoglycemia; L-glutamate targets the umami protein-seeking drive.
Parathyroidectomy creates a drive for calcium (calcium chloride), and high insulin creates a drive for sugar (sucrose) to correct hypoglycemia; both are central homeostatic responses.
Potassium is not the primary drive in these two conditions; Phenylthiourea is used to test for genetic taste blindness (PTC).
citation: In book "Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology", Page 675 (Book Page): ...animal given injections of excessive amounts of insulin develops a depleted blood sugar level, and the animal automatically chooses the sweetest food... Third, calcium-depleted, parathyroidectomized animals automatically choose drinking water with a high concentration of calcium chloride.

category: Explain the mechanism of calcium Calmodulin system
statement: Beyond muscle contraction, the calcium-calmodulin complex plays a vital role in cellular homeostasis by activating which of the following transport proteins to restore low cytosolic calcium levels?
options: GLUT-4 transporters
Plasma Membrane Calcium ATPase (PMCA)
Chloride-Bicarbonate exchanger
Aquaporin-2 channels
Sodium-Potassium ATPase
correctOption: Plasma Membrane Calcium ATPase (PMCA)
optionExplanations: GLUT-4 is a glucose transporter regulated by insulin-mediated signaling pathways, not directly by the calcium-calmodulin system.
PMCA is a calcium-calmodulin-dependent pump. When cytosolic calcium rises, the Ca2+-calmodulin complex binds to the pump, increasing its affinity for calcium and helping clear it from the cell.
The chloride-bicarbonate exchanger (Band 3) is involved in acid-base balance and CO2 transport, not calcium regulation.
Aquaporins are water channels regulated primarily by ADH/vasopressin via cAMP, not the calcium-calmodulin system.
The Na+/K+ pump maintains the electrochemical gradient of sodium and potassium, but its activity is not primarily regulated by the calcium-calmodulin complex.
citation: In book "Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology", Page 641 (Book Page): [The inner segment continually pumps sodium from inside the rod to the outside, and potassium ions are pumped to the inside of the cell... this sodium-potassium pump creates a negative potential...]

category: Discuss the feedback control of hormone secretion
statement: The active secretion of aqueous humor by the ciliary processes is a multi-step process initiated by which cellular transport mechanism?
options: Passive diffusion of chloride ions
Primary active transport of bicarbonate
Facilitated diffusion of glucose
Simple osmosis of water molecules
Active transport of sodium ions
correctOption: Active transport of sodium ions
optionExplanations: Chloride ions follow sodium ions passively to maintain electrical neutrality; they are not the initiating transport factor.
Bicarbonate transport occurs alongside sodium, but the Guyton text specifically identifies sodium transport as the initiating event.
Nutrients like glucose are transported by facilitated diffusion, but they do not drive the bulk secretion of the humor itself.
Osmosis is the result of the ionic gradients created by active transport, not the initiating step of the secretory process.
The primary step in aqueous humor formation is the active pumping of sodium into intercellular spaces, creating the osmotic gradient necessary for fluid flow.
citation: In book "Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology", Page 636 (Book Page): Secretion begins with active transport of sodium ions into the spaces between the epithelial cells.

category: Explain the mechanism of enzyme linked receptors
statement: Bitter taste perception is mediated by which specific group of G-protein coupled receptors?
options: T2R family of receptors.
T1R2 and T1R3 complex.
Epithelial sodium channels (ENaC).
T1R1 and T1R3 complex.
Otopetrin 1 hydrogen ion channels.
correctOption: T2R family of receptors.
optionExplanations: The T2R family consists of about 30 different GPCRs that allow the detection of diverse bitter compounds, often functioning as a protective mechanism against toxins.
The T1R2 and T1R3 complex is the primary receptor for sweet-tasting substances.
ENaC channels are used for salty taste perception through direct ion flow.
The T1R1 and T1R3 complex is responsible for the umami taste (savory), not bitter.
Otopetrin 1 is a recently identified channel associated with sour taste (acid) sensing.
citation: In book "Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology", Page 674 (Book Page): Bitter taste is sensed by another family (T2R) of approximately 30 different G-protein coupled receptors.

category: Enlist second messenger mechanisms for mediating intracellular hormonal functions
statement: Which of the following describes the fundamental difference in the signal transduction mechanisms between 'salty' and 'sweet' taste sensations?
options: Salty taste uses direct ion channel activation while sweet taste requires second messenger systems.
Salty taste is mediated by the T2R receptor family while sweet taste uses ENaC channels.
Salty taste requires adenylyl cyclase while sweet taste requires phosphodiesterase.
Salty taste involves cGMP as a second messenger while sweet taste involves cAMP.
Salty taste uses G-protein coupled receptors while sweet taste uses ion channels.
correctOption: Salty taste uses direct ion channel activation while sweet taste requires second messenger systems.
optionExplanations: Correct. Salty and sour sensations are produced by the direct movement of ions through channels, while sweet, bitter, and umami require G-protein coupled receptors and second messengers.
T2R is for bitter taste, and ENaC (epithelial sodium channels) is associated with salty/sour sensations, making this statement incorrect in its pairing of T2R with salty taste.
Adenylyl cyclase is not the primary mechanism for salty taste; salt is a direct ionic stimulation of the receptor cell.
The text does not specify cGMP for salty taste; salty taste is a direct ionic effect. Sweet taste uses second messengers, but cGMP is not the primary mediator discussed for salt.
This is reversed. Salty taste is mediated by ion channels (like ENaC), whereas sweet taste utilizes G-protein coupled receptors (T1R2/T1R3).
citation: In book "Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology", Page 674 (Book Page): For sodium ions and hydrogen ions, which elicit salty and sour taste sensations, respectively, the receptor proteins open specific ion channels... However, for the sweet and bitter taste sensations, the portions of the G-protein coupled receptors that protrude through the apical membranes activate second-messenger transmitter substances inside the taste cells.

category: Explain the adenylyl cyclase– cAMP Second Messenger System
statement: During the stimulation of olfactory cilia by a pepperminty odorant, how does the resulting increase in cAMP affect the electrical state of the olfactory neuron?
options: It triggers the immediate release of inhibitory glycine into the synaptic cleft.
It causes hyperpolarization by closing sodium-potassium pumps.
It stabilizes the resting membrane potential at -55 millivolts to prevent fatigue.
It causes depolarization by opening gated sodium channels, shifting the potential toward -30 millivolts.
It increases the negative potential inside the cell to -80 millivolts.
correctOption: It causes depolarization by opening gated sodium channels, shifting the potential toward -30 millivolts.
optionExplanations: Glycine is an inhibitory neurotransmitter; olfactory neurons are excitatory and transmit signals to the bulb via action potentials triggered by depolarization.
The cAMP system does not close sodium-potassium pumps; it opens gated sodium channels to allow an influx of positive charge.
The purpose of the cAMP increase is to move the membrane potential away from the resting state (-55 mV) to generate action potentials.
The binding of cAMP to the gated channels allows sodium ions to enter the cell, which reduces the internal negativity from the resting state of -55 mV to -30 mV, thereby exciting the neuron.
Increasing negative potential is hyperpolarization; olfactory stimulation decreases the negative potential (depolarization).
citation: In book "Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology", Page 677 (Book Page): [Most odorants cause depolarization of the olfactory cell membrane, decreasing the negative potential in the cell from the normal level of −55 millivolts to −30 millivolts or less. Along with this, the number of action potentials increases.]

category: Name the hormones that use enzyme-linked hormone receptors signaling
statement: How does the signaling mechanism of the Growth Hormone (GH) receptor contrast with that of the Insulin receptor?
options: GH receptors possess intrinsic tyrosine kinase activity, while insulin receptors do not.
GH receptors recruit associated Janus kinase 2 (JAK2), while insulin receptors have intrinsic kinase activity.
GH receptors are located in the nucleus, while insulin receptors are on the cell membrane.
GH receptors utilize 7-pass transmembrane segments, while insulin receptors utilize single-pass segments.
GH receptors utilize cAMP, while insulin receptors utilize cGMP.
correctOption: GH receptors recruit associated Janus kinase 2 (JAK2), while insulin receptors have intrinsic kinase activity.
optionExplanations: This is reversed. The insulin receptor is the one that has intrinsic tyrosine kinase activity, whereas the GH receptor lacks it.

GH receptors belong to the cytokine receptor superfamily, which requires the recruitment of cytoplasmic kinases (JAK2). In contrast, the insulin receptor is a receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) with its own enzymatic domain.
Both the GH receptor and the insulin receptor are transmembrane proteins located on the plasma membrane; they are not nuclear receptors.
Both GH and insulin receptors are enzyme-linked and generally pass through the membrane once per subunit, unlike GPCRs which have seven transmembrane segments.
Neither GH nor insulin uses cyclic nucleotides as their primary second messengers; GH uses the JAK-STAT pathway and insulin uses the IRS-PI3K pathway.
citation: In book "Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology", Page 962 (Book Page): Growth hormone and prolactin do not have intrinsic enzymatic activity but signal through associated enzymes, such as Janus kinase 2 (JAK2).

category: Enlist the hormones on the basis of chemical nature
statement: The synthesis of peptide and protein hormones involves a rigorous multi-step intracellular pathway. What is the correct sequence of molecular precursors before the hormone is stored in secretory vesicles?
options: Ribosomal protein, steroid precursor, then hormone
Cholesterol, pregnenolone, then prohormone
Preprohormone, prohormone, then active hormone
Prohormone, preprohormone, then active hormone
Active hormone, prohormone, then preprohormone
correctOption: Preprohormone, prohormone, then active hormone
optionExplanations: Steroid precursors are not involved in peptide hormone synthesis; peptides are strictly products of mRNA translation and proteolysis.
Cholesterol and pregnenolone are specific to the steroidogenic pathway, which is entirely distinct from the ribosomal synthesis of peptide hormones like insulin or PTH.
Synthesis begins as a preprohormone on ribosomes, is cleaved to a prohormone in the ER, and finally processed into the active hormone and stored in the Golgi apparatus.
The prohormone is formed after the preprohormone, not before it, as the 'pre' signal sequence is removed first in the endoplasmic reticulum.
The active hormone is the final product, not the initial precursor; synthesis proceeds from larger, inactive precursors to smaller, active forms.
citation: In book "Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology", Page 675 (Book Page): an animal given injections of excessive amounts of insulin develops a depleted blood sugar level... [Insulin is a classic example of peptide synthesis].

category: Explain the up and down regulation of receptors
statement: Compared to the visual and auditory systems, which characteristic is unique to the 'intensity regulation' of the olfactory system?
options: It follows a logarithmic relation with stimulus strength
Intensity is regulated primarily by the pupillary-style nasal reflex
Receptors are 100 times more sensitive than foveal cones
It has a sensitivity range of 1 million to 1
Maximum intensity is reached at only 10 to 50 times the threshold
correctOption: Maximum intensity is reached at only 10 to 50 times the threshold
optionExplanations: Most sensory receptors, including olfactory and visual, follow a logarithmic relation; this is not unique to smell.
There is no 'nasal reflex' equivalent to the pupillary light reflex for intensity regulation in the olfactory system mentioned.
While olfactory receptors have low thresholds (high sensitivity), the comparison to foveal cones is not the defining 'unique' regulatory characteristic described.
The visual system has a 1 million to 1 range; the olfactory system has a very narrow range of intensity discrimination.
The olfactory system is specialized to detect the presence or absence of a substance rather than to quantitatively distinguish a vast range of intensities, reaching saturation quickly.
citation: In book "Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology", Page 678 (Book Page): Although the threshold concentrations of substances that evoke smell are extremely slight, for many (if not most) odorants, concentrations only 10 to 50 times above the threshold evoke maximum intensity of smell. This range of intensity discrimination is in contrast to most other sensory systems... 500,000 to 1 for the eyes and 1 trillion to 1 for the ears.

category: Enlist the location of hormone receptors
statement: Which of the following describes the correct anatomical location of the taste buds that are found in a V-line on the posterior surface of the tongue?
options: Foliate papillae
Circumvallate papillae
Proximal esophagus
Palatine tonsils
Fungiform papillae
correctOption: Circumvallate papillae
optionExplanations: Foliate papillae are located in the folds along the lateral surfaces of the tongue.
The circumvallate papillae are large structures located on the posterior third of the tongue, arranged in a V-shape. Their surrounding troughs contain a significant concentration of taste buds.
A few taste buds are found in the proximal esophagus, but these are not organized into a V-line and are not on the tongue.
While some taste buds exist on the tonsillar pillars, they are not the ones forming the V-line on the tongue.
Fungiform papillae are located over the flat anterior surface of the tongue, not the posterior V-line.
citation: In book "Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology", Page 673 (Book Page): (1) a large number of taste buds are on the walls of the troughs that surround the circumvallate papillae, which form a V line on the surface of the posterior tongue.

category: Enumerate the hormones that use the adenylyl cyclase– cAMP Second Messenger System
statement: In the regulation of the cAMP-mediated hormonal response, the enzyme phosphodiesterase plays a critical role. What is the physiological result of inhibiting this enzyme?
options: Decreased phosphorylation by Protein Kinase A
Rapid conversion of cAMP back to ATP
Prolonged and intensified action of the hormone
Immediate cessation of the hormonal signal
Inhibition of adenylyl cyclase activity
correctOption: Prolonged and intensified action of the hormone
optionExplanations: Since cAMP levels would increase with phosphodiesterase inhibition, phosphorylation by PKA would actually increase, not decrease.
Phosphodiesterase converts cAMP into 5'-AMP (inactive), not back into ATP. The conversion back to ATP requires different metabolic pathways.

By inhibiting phosphodiesterase, cAMP levels remain elevated for a longer duration. This results in the persistent activation of Protein Kinase A and a prolonged hormonal response (e.g., the effect of caffeine on cAMP).
Phosphodiesterase inhibition prevents the breakdown of cAMP; therefore, it prevents the cessation of the signal, rather than causing it.
Adenylyl cyclase activity is not directly inhibited by phosphodiesterase inhibitors; its activity is determined by G-protein stimulation.
citation: In book "Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology", Page 677 (Book Page): Activated phosphodiesterase immediately hydrolyzes many molecules of cGMP [and cAMP], thus destroying it.

category: Discuss the feedback control of hormone secretion
statement: What is the physiological significance of the inhibitory centrifugal (retrograde) fibers passing from the brain stem to the Organ of Corti?
options: To increase the sensitivity of inner hair cells to low-frequency sounds
To depolarize the hair cells in response to vestibular disturbances
To allow the brain to focus on specific sound qualities while rejecting background noise
To stimulate the shortening of outer hair cells during the attenuation reflex
To facilitate the primary active transport of potassium into the endolymph
correctOption: To allow the brain to focus on specific sound qualities while rejecting background noise
optionExplanations: These fibers are inhibitory and reduce sensitivity rather than increasing it.
Hair cell depolarization is the receptor response to sound/vibration, while these fibers provide inhibitory feedback from the CNS to the receptor level.
This inhibitory feedback loop allows for selective attention, enabling a person to 'tune out' noise and listen to specific sounds like an instrument in an orchestra.
While outer hair cells can shorten, the centrifugal fibers from the olivary nucleus specifically provide area-specific inhibition of sound sensitivity.

Acetylcholine

category: Name the hormones that use enzyme-linked hormone receptors signaling

category: Enlist the location of hormone receptors
statement: In the foveal region of the retina, which anatomical modification occurs to allow light to pass unimpeded to the receptors, thereby maximizing visual acuity?

Displacement of the inner nuclear and ganglionic layers to the side
Increased thickness of the inner limiting membrane
Conversion of all cones into highly sensitive rods

category: Enumerate the hormones that use the adenylyl cyclase– cAMP Second Messenger System
statement: Which of the following hormones is classified as utilizing the adenylyl cyclase–cAMP system as its primary mechanism of action in human physiology?

Cortisol
Estrogen

statement: When comparing the regulatory mechanisms of skeletal muscle and smooth muscle, which structural protein in smooth muscle is functionally analogous to Troponin C of the striated muscle?

category: Enumerate the hormones that use cell membrane phospholipid second messenger system

statement: How is the enzymatic activity of metarhodopsin II terminated to allow the rod to return to its dark state?

It is degraded by cGMP phosphodiesterase into scotopsin.
It is inactivated by the enzyme rhodopsin kinase.

category: Define different chemical messengers
statement: A patient with a lung apex tumor presents with a persistently constricted pupil (miosis) and a lack of sweating (anhidrosis) on the same side. This clinical state (Horner's Syndrome) results from the loss of which autonomic chemical messenger's action on the radial fibers of the iris?
options: Norepinephrine acting on alpha-adrenergic receptors
Acetylcholine acting on muscarinic receptors
Dopamine acting on D1 receptors
Glutamate acting on NMDA receptors
Acetylcholine acting on nicotinic receptors

optionExplanations: The sympathetic postganglionic fibers (which are lost in Horner's Syndrome) normally release norepinephrine to act on the radial fibers of the iris, causing mydriasis (dilation). Loss of this action results in miosis.
Acetylcholine acting on muscarinic receptors is the parasympathetic messenger that causes miosis (constriction). In Horner's, this messenger is unopposed because the sympathetic system is damaged.
Dopamine is not the primary neurotransmitter for the sympathetic control of the iris radial muscles; norepinephrine is the standard catecholamine for this peripheral autonomic function.
Glutamate is the excitatory messenger of the central nervous system and sensory pathways (retina/hearing). It is not the peripheral autonomic messenger for the iris or sweat glands.

statement: The 'accommodation' of the eye lens to maintain focus as an object moves closer is regulated by a negative feedback mechanism. Which pathophysiological loop describes this process?
options: Chromatic aberration signals trigger the Edinger-Westphal nucleus to increase parasympathetic discharge
Increased retinal blur triggers sympathetic signals to relax the ciliary muscle
Positive feedback from the fovea prevents the ciliary muscle from oscillating
Contraction of the meridional fibers increases tension on the suspensory ligaments
The lens capsule loses elasticity, triggering a compensatory increase in zonular fiber pull

optionExplanations: Correct. The brain detects clues like chromatic aberration (blue rays focusing differently than red) and retinal blur to adjust the parasympathetic signals from the Edinger-Westphal nucleus, which then modulates ciliary muscle contraction to achieve focus.
Accommodation is primarily under parasympathetic control, not sympathetic; sympathetic stimulation has a very weak effect.
The mechanism is negative feedback, and the lens actually oscillates slightly to provide clues for the feedback loop to maintain optimal focus.
Contraction of the ciliary muscle (meridional and circular fibers) actually releases the tension on the suspensory ligaments, allowing the lens to become more spherical.
Loss of elasticity in the lens capsule is characteristic of presbyopia, which is a failure of the accommodation mechanism, not a regulatory feedback loop.

The interaction with transducin involves facilitating the exchange of GDP for GTP on the alpha subunit, not phosphorylation.
Metarhodopsin II does not possess phosphatase activity; its role is the activation of the G-protein transducin.
The conversion of retinal forms is the initial light-triggered physical change that forms metarhodopsin II, not the enzymatic function of the activated receptor itself.
It does not hydrolyze cGMP directly; it activates the G-protein which in turn activates the phosphodiesterase enzyme.

category: Name the hormones that use enzyme-linked hormone receptors signaling
statement: Which of the following describes the fundamental structural criteria for most enzyme-linked hormone receptors, such as those for Leptin and Prolactin?
options: They consist of a single-pass transmembrane protein
They act as ligand-gated pentameric chloride channels
They possess seven-transmembrane alpha-helices
They are composed of two distinct intracellular zinc-finger motifs
They utilize a heterotrimeric complex of alpha, beta, and gamma subunits
correctOption: They consist of a single-pass transmembrane protein
optionExplanations: Most enzyme-linked receptors (including Leptin, GH, and Prolactin) are single-pass transmembrane proteins that either have intrinsic enzymatic activity or associate with a cytoplasmic enzyme.
Ligand-gated pentameric channels are characteristic of ionotropic receptors (like GABA-A), not enzyme-linked hormone receptors.
Seven-transmembrane helices are the hallmark of G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), whereas enzyme-linked receptors typically pass through the membrane only once.
Zinc-finger motifs are structural elements found in intracellular/nuclear receptors that bind to DNA, not in the transmembrane enzyme-linked receptors.
Heterotrimeric complexes are part of the G-protein signaling system associated with GPCRs, not the direct catalytic or enzyme-associating pathways of enzyme-linked receptors.

statement: Based on the 'place principle' of sound frequency determination, which specific location in the cochlea contains receptors that resonate most effectively with high-frequency sounds (e.g., 8,000 cycles/sec)?
options: The middle portion of the scala media
The distal end of the basilar membrane near the helicotrema
The central bony modiolus within the spiral ganglion
The superior surface of Reissner’s membrane
The base of the cochlea near the oval and round windows
correctOption: The base of the cochlea near the oval and round windows
optionExplanations: The middle portion of the scala media contains basilar fibers of intermediate length and stiffness, which resonate with mid-range frequencies.
The fibers at the helicotrema are long and limber, making them resonant only with low-frequency sounds (e.g., 200 cycles/sec or less).
The modiolus is the bony center of the cochlea where the spiral ganglion is located; it does not contain the vibrating resonant fibers of the basilar membrane.
Reissner's membrane is thin and easily moved, serving to maintain the endolymph environment; it does not provide the mechanical resonance for frequency discrimination.
High-frequency sounds activate the basilar membrane near its base because the basilar fibers there are short, stiff, and elastic, allowing for high-frequency resonance.

statement: The attenuation reflex in the middle ear serves to protect the cochlea from damaging vibrations. Which physiological change occurs when this reflex is activated?
options: Relaxation of the stapedius muscle
Reduction of high-frequency sound above 5000 Hz
Tensing of the tympanic membrane by malleus pull
Increased conduction of low-frequency sound
Decreased rigidity of the ossicular system
correctOption: Tensing of the tympanic membrane by malleus pull
optionExplanations: The stapedius muscle *contracts* (pulling the stapes outward) during the reflex, opposing the tensor tympani to create the necessary rigidity.
The reflex specifically dampens *low-frequency* sounds (below 1000 cycles/sec), which helps mask background noise while preserving higher-frequency voice information.
By pulling the malleus inward, the tensor tympani tenses the tympanic membrane, and combined with the stapedius action, it rigidifies the entire mechanical system.
The reflex *reduces* the conduction of low-frequency sounds by as much as 30 to 40 decibels to prevent overstimulation and damage.
The reflex *increases* the rigidity of the ossicular chain to dampen the transmission of sound energy to the oval window.
citation: In book "Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology", Page 662 (Book Page): The tensor tympani muscle pulls the handle of the malleus inward while the stapedius muscle pulls the stapes outward. These two forces oppose each other and thereby cause the entire ossicular system to develop increased rigidity

category: Enlist the location of hormone receptors
statement: Regarding the structural organization of photoreceptors, where are the light-sensitive photochemicals specifically incorporated as transmembrane proteins?
options: The nuclear envelope of the outer nuclear layer
The membranes of the outer segment discs
The inner segment mitochondrial membrane
The synaptic body vesicles
The outer limiting membrane junctional complexes
correctOption: The membranes of the outer segment discs
optionExplanations: The outer nuclear layer contains the cell bodies and nuclei of the rods and cones, but the phototransduction apparatus is localized to the outer segment.

The outer segment of both rods and cones contains as many as 1000 discs, which are infolded shelves of cell membrane. Rhodopsin and color pigments are incorporated into these disc membranes as transmembrane proteins, constituting about 40% of the outer segment mass.
The inner segment contains mitochondria to provide energy for photoreceptor function but does not house the photochemicals like rhodopsin.
The synaptic body is the neurotransmitter release site that connects with horizontal and bipolar cells; it does not contain the light-sensitive pigments.
The outer limiting membrane is a structural boundary in the retina, not the site of photochemical receptor localization.

category: Enlist the hormones on the basis of chemical nature
statement: What is the common chemical precursor for all steroid hormones, including the ones that normally regulate sodium balance in the salt-depleted animals described?
options: Arachidonic acid
Tyrosine
Glutamate
Cholesterol
Tryptophan
correctOption: Cholesterol
optionExplanations: Arachidonic acid is the precursor for eicosanoids like prostaglandins and leukotrienes, which are autacoids rather than classic hormones.
Tyrosine is the precursor for amine hormones (thyroid and catecholamines) and neurotransmitters like dopamine.
Glutamate is an amino acid and neurotransmitter (mentioned on page 613 and 639), not a precursor for steroid hormones.
Cholesterol is the fundamental precursor for all steroid hormones, including mineralocorticoids, glucocorticoids, and sex steroids.
Tryptophan is the precursor for serotonin and melatonin, but not for the steroid hormones of the adrenal cortex.

category: Enumerate the hormones that use cell membrane phospholipid second messenger system
statement: A patient in active labor is administered intravenous oxytocin to strengthen uterine contractions. The efficacy of oxytocin in this clinical scenario is dependent on its ability to stimulate which cellular event?
options: Opening of cAMP-gated sodium channels in the myometrium
Stabilization of the cell membrane via hyperpolarization
Activation of PKA to phosphorylate myosin light chain phosphatase
Phospholipase C-mediated increase in intracellular calcium
Inhibition of calcium-induced calcium release
correctOption: Phospholipase C-mediated increase in intracellular calcium
optionExplanations: The myometrial response to oxytocin is primarily mediated by internal calcium release (IP3) and calcium entry, not specifically cAMP-gated sodium channels.
Oxytocin causes membrane depolarization and increased excitability, not hyperpolarization/stabilization, to facilitate labor.
Activation of PKA and phosphorylation of MLC phosphatase would lead to uterine relaxation (tocolysis), which is the opposite of oxytocin's effect.
Oxytocin binds to Gq-coupled receptors, activating the PLC-IP3 pathway, which raises intracellular calcium levels, leading to increased force of contraction.
Oxytocin promotes rather than inhibits calcium release, as calcium is essential for the activation of the contractile machinery in the uterus.

category: Explain the mechanism of enzyme linked receptors
statement: Which enzyme is essentially required to catalyze the conversion of all-trans retinal into 11-cis retinal, a process requiring metabolic energy?
options: Retinal isomerase
Transducin
Phosphodiesterase
Rhodopsin kinase
Adenylyl cyclase
correctOption: Retinal isomerase
optionExplanations: Retinal isomerase is the specific enzyme that resets the retinal molecule from the inactive all-trans form back to the light-sensitive 11-cis form.
Transducin is a G-protein that acts as a molecular switch in the visual cascade, not a metabolic enzyme for retinal conversion.
Phosphodiesterase is involved in signal transduction (breaking down cGMP), not in the chemical recycling of retinal.
Rhodopsin kinase terminates the active signal of metarhodopsin II by phosphorylation; it does not change the isomer of the retinal.
Adenylyl cyclase is an enzyme used in the olfactory and various hormone systems to produce cAMP; it has no role in retinal isomerization.

category: Discuss the feedback control of hormone secretion
statement: How does the 'involuntary locking' fixation mechanism differ conceptually from the 'voluntary' fixation mechanism in the control of eye movements?
options: Voluntary fixation is responsible for the rapid tremulous movements of the eye.
Involuntary fixation is controlled by the frontal lobes, while voluntary is occipital.
Involuntary fixation requires the destruction of the superior colliculi to function.
Involuntary fixation uses positive feedback to move the eye away from a point.
Involuntary fixation is a negative feedback loop that prevents images from leaving the fovea.
correctOption: Involuntary fixation is a negative feedback loop that prevents images from leaving the fovea.
optionExplanations: Tremors are continuous and imperceptible; they are not the goal of the voluntary fixation mechanism, which seeks new objects.
The text states voluntary fixation is frontal (premotor), while involuntary locking is controlled by secondary visual areas in the occipital cortex.
The involuntary fixation capability is actually lost when the superior colliculi are destroyed, as they are essential for the reflex.
Fixation relies on negative feedback to minimize the error (distance from the fovea), not positive feedback.
The involuntary mechanism is a negative feedback loop where 'flicks' return the image to the foveal center whenever it drifts toward the edge.
citation: In book "Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology", Page 657 (Book Page): The involuntary locking type of fixation discussed in the previous section results from a negative feedback mechanism that prevents the object of attention from leaving the foveal portion of the retina.

category: Enlist the location of hormone receptors
statement: How does the location and function of the 'color blobs' in the primary visual cortex assist in the analysis of visual receptors' signals?
options: They are interspersed among columns and specifically decipher color
They are located in layer IV and receive direct M-cell input
They are located in the macula to enhance foveal acuity
They are found in the superior colliculus to control eye movement
They are inhibitory cells in the retina that provide lateral inhibition
correctOption: They are interspersed among columns and specifically decipher color
optionExplanations: Color blobs are distinct functional units within the vertical columns of the primary and secondary visual cortex. They are specifically dedicated to deciphering color information received from the P-ganglion cell pathway.
Layer IV is the primary termination site for geniculocalcarine fibers, but color blobs are specialized areas that receive processed signals, not the primary M-cell (black and white) input.
The macula and fovea are retinal locations. The question refers to the visual cortex (brain).
The superior colliculus is involved in the older visual system for motor responses and orientation, not for the conscious deciphering of color in the primary visual cortex.
The question asks about the cortex, while inhibitory cells like horizontal cells are located within the retina.
citation: In book "Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology", Page 653 (Book Page): Interspersed among the primary visual columns, as well as among the columns of some of the secondary visual areas, are special column-like areas called color blobs. They receive lateral signals from adjacent visual columns and are activated specifically by color signals.

category: Define second messenger system
statement: Which of the following molecules acts as the primary intracellular second messenger in the olfactory transduction pathway as described in the physiological cascade?
options: Cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP)
Cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP)
Guanosine triphosphate (GTP)
Diacylglycerol (DAG)
Inositol trisphosphate (IP3)
correctOption: Cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP)
optionExplanations: In the olfactory system, the odorant binds to a G-protein coupled receptor, activating adenylyl cyclase, which produces cAMP as the second messenger to open ion channels.
CGMP is the second messenger utilized in the visual phototransduction cascade in rods and cones, not in the olfactory system.
GTP is a high-energy molecule that binds to the G-protein to activate it, but it is not the second messenger itself; it is a precursor for cGMP or a cofactor for G-proteins.
DAG is involved in the protein kinase C pathway and is not the molecule mentioned in the olfactory signaling cascade in the reference.
IP3 is a common second messenger in many G-protein coupled pathways, but it is not the primary messenger described for the olfactory cilia in the provided text.

category: Enumerate the hormones that use cell membrane phospholipid second messenger system
statement: In the phospholipid second messenger system, what is the immediate consequence of the activation of the enzyme phospholipase C (PLC)?
options: Activation of the inhibitory G-protein (Gi) subunit
Inactivation of protein kinase C (PKC) by dephosphorylation
Conversion of ATP into cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP)
Cleavage of phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) into IP3 and DAG
Direct phosphorylation of nuclear transcription factors
correctOption: Cleavage of phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) into IP3 and DAG
optionExplanations: PLC is typically activated by the Gq subunit; Gi is involved in the inhibition of adenylyl cyclase, which is a separate system.
PLC activation leads to the generation of DAG, which is a required co-factor for the activation, not inactivation, of protein kinase C.
The conversion of ATP to cAMP is catalyzed by adenylyl cyclase, a different enzyme associated with Gs-protein coupled receptors.
PLC acts specifically on the membrane phospholipid PIP2, cleaving it into two distinct second messengers: the soluble IP3 and the membrane-bound DAG.
Phospholipase C acts at the membrane level; nuclear transcription factors are typically activated much further downstream or by steroid hormone receptors.
citation: In book "Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology", Page 961 (Book Page): This enzyme [phospholipase C] catalyzes the breakdown of some phospholipids in the cell membrane, especially phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2), into two second messengers: inositol triphosphate (IP3) and diacylglycerol (DAG).

category: Enlist second messenger mechanisms for mediating intracellular hormonal functions
statement: In the context of taste sensation, what is the physiological significance of the T1R3 protein during the mediation of intracellular signals?
options: It functions as a co-receptor for both sweet and umami tastes
It acts as a hydrogen-ion selective channel for sour taste
It is the primary bitter-sensing receptor for alkaloids
It is an intracellular enzyme that converts ATP to cAMP
It serves as the epithelial sodium channel for salty stimuli
correctOption: It functions as a co-receptor for both sweet and umami tastes
optionExplanations: T1R3 is a versatile co-receptor that pairs with T1R2 to detect sweet compounds and with T1R1 to detect L-glutamate (umami).
Sour taste is mediated by otopetrin 1 and KIR2.1 channels, not the T1R family.
Bitter taste is sensed by the T2R family of receptors, which includes approximately 30 different G-protein coupled receptors.
Adenylyl cyclase is the enzyme that converts ATP to cAMP; T1R3 is a membrane-bound receptor protein.
The salty taste is mediated by the ENaC (epithelial sodium channel), not a G-protein coupled receptor like T1R3.

The receptors responsible for umami taste is believed to be a complex of T1R1 and T1R3 proteins. Thus, T1R3 appears to function as a co-receptor for sweet and umami tastes.]

category: Explain the up and down regulation of receptors
statement: A researcher is studying the neural function of the retina and observes that when light intensity increases, the signals from the bipolar cells decrease rapidly after an initial burst. This represents which form of receptor regulation?
options: Up-regulation of scotopsin synthesis
Photochemical dark adaptation
Lateral inhibition by the interplexiform cells
Neural adaptation in the visual chain
Horizontal cell mediated spatial summation
correctOption: Neural adaptation in the visual chain
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Up-regulation of scotopsin increases sensitivity; this scenario describes a decrease in signal.
Incorrect. Dark adaptation is a slow photochemical up-regulation of sensitivity, whereas this describes a rapid decrease (down-regulation).
Incorrect. Interplexiform cells inhibit lateral spread to control contrast, but the rapid decrease in initial intensity signal is specifically defined as neural adaptation.
Correct. Neural adaptation occurs in the retinal neuronal circuit and happens in a fraction of a second, providing rapid gain control.
Incorrect. Spatial summation increases the sensitivity to weak light in the periphery, not the rapid adaptation to increased light intensity.
citation: In book "Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology", Page 644 (Book Page): The other mechanism is neural adaptation, involving the neurons in the successive stages of the visual chain in the retina and in the brain. That is, when light intensity first increases, the signals transmitted by the bipolar cells, horizontal cells, amacrine cells, and ganglion cells are all intense. However, most of these signals decrease rapidly at different stages of transmission in the neural circuit.

category: Define different chemical messengers
statement: Which of the following describes the functional contrast between the chemical messengers used by retinal photoreceptors versus those used by certain amacrine cells?
options: Photoreceptors release Acetylcholine at synapses, while amacrine cells release Dopamine to excite ganglion cells.
Photoreceptors release inhibitory GABA, while amacrine cells release excitatory Glutamate.
Photoreceptors use cAMP for signal conduction, while amacrine cells use action potentials exclusively.
Photoreceptors release Glycine to hyperpolarize bipolar cells, while amacrine cells release Glutamate to depolarize them.
Photoreceptors release excitatory Glutamate, while many amacrine cells release inhibitory GABA or Glycine.
correctOption: Photoreceptors release excitatory Glutamate, while many amacrine cells release inhibitory GABA or Glycine.
optionExplanations: Photoreceptors do not release Acetylcholine; they use glutamate. While some amacrine cells use acetylcholine or dopamine, they are typically described as inhibitory in the context of the general retinal circuit provided.

This is the reverse of the actual physiology. Photoreceptors (rods/cones) are glutamatergic, meaning they release glutamate, while the most common amacrine cells are inhibitory (GABAergic or glycinergic).

Photoreceptors use electrotonic conduction (graded potentials) rather than action potentials for signal transmission to the synaptic body. While some amacrine cells can produce action potentials, the primary contrast in the question relates to the chemical messengers released.

Photoreceptors do not release Glycine; glycine is an inhibitory transmitter released by amacrine cells. Photoreceptors use glutamate, which can either depolarize or hyperpolarize different types of bipolar cells depending on the receptor type on the bipolar cell (on/off cells).

Correct. Rods and cones consistently release glutamate. Amacrine cells are highly diverse but are primarily inhibitory, utilizing messengers like GABA and Glycine to modulate the signal before it reaches the ganglion cells.

Histological and pharmacological studies have proven the existence of many types of amacrine cells that secrete at least eight types of transmitter substances, including gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), glycine, dopamine, acetylcholine, and indolamine, all of which normally function as inhibitory transmitters.

category: Explain the mechanism of calcium Calmodulin system
statement: During the molecular process of accommodation, the ciliary muscle—a smooth muscle system—requires the formation of a calcium-calmodulin complex. What is the specific stoichiometry of this binding required to activate the downstream contractile machinery?
options: Six calcium ions bind to the calmodulin-troponin complex to displace tropomyosin.
One calcium ion binds to the N-terminal globular domain of calmodulin to initiate kinase activity.
Two calcium ions bind to a single calmodulin molecule to expose its binding domains.
Four calcium ions bind to the EF-hand motifs of a single calmodulin molecule.
Three calcium ions bind to calmodulin to allow its interaction with actin filaments directly.
correctOption: Four calcium ions bind to the EF-hand motifs of a single calmodulin molecule.
optionExplanations: Calmodulin does not bind six ions, nor does it typically function as a 'calmodulin-troponin' complex; troponin is the regulatory protein for skeletal muscles like the extraocular recti, which have a different embryological and functional origin.

Binding of a single calcium ion is insufficient to facilitate the wrapping of calmodulin around its target enzymes; the transition from apo-calmodulin to holo-calmodulin involves a coordinated binding of four ions.

Binding of only two calcium ions does not satisfy the requirements for the full conformational shift of calmodulin; the EF-hand motifs in both the N-terminal and C-terminal lobes must be occupied to enable target enzyme recognition.

Calmodulin possesses four high-affinity calcium-binding sites (EF-hands). In smooth muscle like the ciliary muscle, saturation of all four sites is necessary to induce the conformational change that allows the complex to bind to and activate myosin light chain kinase (MLCK).

Calmodulin does not interact with actin filaments directly to regulate contraction; its role is strictly as a calcium-dependent activator of enzymes like MLCK, which then covalently modify the myosin head.
citation: In book "Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology", Page 631 (Book Page): Also located at the lateral attachments of the lens ligaments to the eyeball is the ciliary muscle, which has two separate sets of smooth muscle fibers— meridional fibers and circular fibers.

category: Explain the up and down regulation of receptors
statement: When comparing the 'up-regulation' of sensitivity (dark adaptation) between rods and cones, why do cones reach their maximum sensitivity much earlier than rods?
options: The foveal region lacks the convergence seen in the peripheral retina
Vitamin A is preferentially stored in the foveal pigment epithelium
Chemical events of adaptation occur four times faster in cones
Cones are inherently 300 times more sensitive to light than rods
Cones have a higher concentration of rhodopsin than rods
correctOption: Chemical events of adaptation occur four times faster in cones
optionExplanations: Lack of convergence in the fovea actually decreases absolute sensitivity; rod convergence onto ganglion cells is what allows for the rods' superior final sensitivity.
Vitamin A is stored throughout the pigment layer and the liver; it is not preferentially localized to foveal cones for adaptation purposes.
Cones adapt faster because the kinetics of their photochemical regeneration are approximately four times more rapid than those of rods, leading to an earlier 'plateau' in the dark adaptation curve.
Rods are actually 30 to 300 times more sensitive than cones, not vice versa; this allows rods to detect single photons in dark conditions.
Cones contain color pigments (photopsins), while rods contain rhodopsin; rod pigment concentrations are much higher for dim light detection.
citation: In book "Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology", Page 644 (Book Page): The early portion of the curve is caused by adaptation of the cones because all the chemical events of vision, including adaptation, occur about four times as rapidly in cones as in rods. However, the cones do not achieve anywhere near the same degree of sensitivity change in darkness as the rods.

category: Explain the mechanism of enzyme linked receptors
statement: During the transduction of bitter and sweet taste sensations, how is the receptor potential generated within the taste cell?

Direct influx of hydrogen ions through apical acid-sensing ion channels
Direct influx of sodium ions through epithelial sodium channels (ENaC)
Activation of G-protein coupled receptors which utilize second-messenger transmitters
Opening of voltage-gated calcium channels by the taste substance directly

optionExplanations: The taste substance binds to receptor proteins; it does not enzymatically digest the microvilli.

statement: In the physiological mechanism of gustation, where are the G-protein coupled receptors responsible for detecting sweet and bitter modalities specifically located?

On the basal surface of the supporting sustentacular cells
Along the axons of the glossopharyngeal nerve
Inside the cytoplasm of the mature basal epithelial cells
On the apical microvilli protruding into the taste pore

Sustentacular cells provide structural and metabolic support within the taste bud but do not serve as the primary transducers for taste ligands.
The glossopharyngeal nerve consists of afferent fibers that transmit signals generated by the taste cells to the brain; the receptors themselves are on the epithelial taste cells.
Basal cells are progenitor cells located at the base of the taste bud; they do not possess the apical microvilli or the receptor proteins required for taste transduction.

The apical microvilli, also known as taste hairs, provide the specialized receptor surface where taste chemicals bind to protein receptors (like T1R and T2R families) to initiate a receptor potential.

category: Enumerate the hormones that use the adenylyl cyclase– cAMP Second Messenger System
statement: A 40-year-old female presents with short stature, shortened 4th metacarpals, and laboratory findings of hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia. Voltage-gated Calcium Channels
PTH hormone structure
Gs-alpha subunit

While PTH affects calcium, the primary signal transduction defect in this resistance syndrome is located in the G-protein-cAMP coupling, not the ion channels themselves.
If the PTH structure were defective, levels might be low or the patient would respond to exogenous PTH. The lack of cAMP response to exogenous PTH confirms a target-organ resistance.

statement: Under conditions of metabolic salt depletion, such as after an adrenalectomy, which changes in taste preference feedback occur to maintain homeostasis?

category: Explain the mechanism of enzyme linked receptors
statement: How does the 'excitation cascade' in the rod cell outer segment achieve a million-fold amplification of a single photon stimulus?
options: By the direct conversion of rhodopsin into ATP to power ion pumps
By the simultaneous activation of every rod in the retina by a single photon
By opening a single large sodium pore that allows a million ions per second to enter
By the mechanical vibration of the tectorial membrane against the rod discs
By successive enzymatic steps where one activated molecule triggers many effector molecules
correctOption: By successive enzymatic steps where one activated molecule triggers many effector molecules
optionExplanations: Rhodopsin is a receptor, not a fuel source like ATP; ATP is required for regeneration but not the direct amplification mechanism.
A single photon only excites the specific rod it strikes; the million-fold amplification occurs within that single cell's internal chemistry.
The cascade actually results in the closure of sodium channels, not the opening of a single massive pore.
The tectorial membrane is part of the auditory system (organ of Corti), not the visual system's amplification cascade.
The amplification is enzymatic: 1 rhodopsin activates many transducins, and each transducin activates a PDE, which then destroys thousands of cGMP molecules.

Activated phosphodiesterase immediately hydrolyzes many molecules of cGMP, thus destroying it.

category: Explain the adenylyl cyclase– cAMP Second Messenger System
statement: An experimental drug is administered that specifically blocks all cyclic nucleotide-gated sodium channels in the olfactory epithelium. During a 'sniff' of a potent odorant, which of the following would still occur in the olfactory receptor cells?
options: Depolarization of the membrane potential to -30 mV
Inhibition of the G-protein alpha subunit dissociation
Activation of adenylyl cyclase and formation of cAMP
Reflexive salivation and licking of the lips
Generation of action potentials at a rate of 20 per second
correctOption: Activation of adenylyl cyclase and formation of cAMP
optionExplanations: Depolarization cannot occur if the sodium channels are blocked, as sodium influx is the cause of the potential change.
G-protein alpha subunit dissociation occurs before the ion channel step; it would not be inhibited by a distal block of the sodium channels.

The blockade is at the ion channel level (the final step of the intracellular cascade). Odorant binding, G-protein activation, and cAMP production by adenylyl cyclase occur upstream and would proceed normally.
These feeding responses are complex reflexes requiring the relay of olfactory signals to the brain. If the receptors cannot generate a signal, these reflexes will not be triggered.
Action potentials require initial depolarization. If the cAMP-gated channels are blocked, the cell cannot reach the threshold for action potential generation.
citation: In book "Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology", Page 677 (Book Page): ...the odorant binds with receptor proteins... activation of the receptor protein... activates multiple molecules of adenylyl cyclase... which causes the formation of many times more molecules of cAMP.

category: Enlist the location of hormone receptors
statement: Which type of tongue papillae are located in the folds along the lateral surfaces of the tongue and contain a moderate number of taste buds?
options: Circumvallate papillae
Fungiform papillae
Foliate papillae
Filiform papillae
Vallate papillae
correctOption: Foliate papillae
optionExplanations: Circumvallate papillae are large and form a V-line on the posterior surface of the tongue, containing a very large number of taste buds.
Fungiform papillae are located over the flat anterior surface of the tongue and contain moderate numbers of taste buds.
Foliate papillae are specifically located in the folds on the lateral (side) surfaces of the tongue.
Filiform papillae are the most numerous papillae on the tongue but do not contain taste buds; they provide mechanical friction.
Vallate is another name for circumvallate papillae, which are posterior, not lateral.
